title: Gateau chocolat pruneaux
subtitle: A dense French chocolate cake with brandy-soaked prunes throughout the batter
excerpt: Gateau chocolat pruneaux is a French chocolate cake with very little flour and a high proportion of dark chocolate and butter. The brandy-soaked prunes sink into the batter and give the finished cake a deep, moist sweetness. It slices cleanly the next day and keeps for four to five days.
sourceNotes: The combination of dark chocolate and Agen prunes is a classic South-West French pairing found across the cookery of Gascon and the Lot-et-Garonne. The recipe form described here follows the style documented in French regional cookery literature: chocolate-dense, barely-flour cakes with prunes as a textural and flavour element.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze individually. Thaw at room temperature for 1 hour.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made the day before; the texture firms to a perfect fudgy density overnight. Store covered at room temperature for up to 5 days.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 180 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 165 degrees Celsius. The cake should look barely set in the centre when removed; it firms as it cools.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pitted prunes soaked in brandy or Armagnac for at least 30 minutes before use. The spirit plumps the fruit and adds a layer of warmth and complexity to chocolate cakes and tarts. Agen prunes from South-West France are the traditional choice; Californian prunes work well and are easier to find in the UK.

content.text: need at least 30 minutes to plump in the brandy before the batter goes in. The cake has very little flour: its structure comes from the eggs and the set chocolate. The centre should look barely set when you take it from the oven; it firms to a fudgy density as it cools.

items.prepNote: for dusting the tin and finishing (optional)

content.text: Put the pitted prunes in a bowl, pour the brandy over them, and stir to coat. Leave to soak for at least 30 minutes. The prunes can be soaked overnight; they will plump further and the brandy flavour will deepen.
Preheat the oven to 180 degrees Celsius. Grease a 20 cm round cake tin and dust with cocoa powder.
Melt the chocolate and butter together in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of simmering water, stirring until smooth. Remove from heat and leave to cool for 5 minutes.
Whisk the sugar into the warm chocolate mixture. Add the eggs one at a time, whisking well after each. Sift in the flour and salt and fold until just combined. Do not overmix.
Pour half the batter into the tin. Arrange the soaked prunes in a single layer over the batter, spacing them evenly. Pour the remaining batter over the prunes to cover them.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes. The edges should be set and the centre still has a slight wobble when the tin is gently moved. Cool completely in the tin before turning out; the cake is fragile when warm.

The cake cuts cleanest the day after baking, once the chocolate has had time to firm at room temperature. Run a hot knife under hot water, wipe dry, and cut. The blade goes through the prunes cleanly rather than dragging.
